v: A typical home in Calgary pays the City three hundred and sixty-nine dollars a month, for property tax, water and waste. The proposed budget would raise that. So how does Calgary compare with other large Canadian cities?

We compared eight cities: Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, Toronto, Ottawa, Winnipeg, Saskatoon and Regina. For each, we took the City property tax on its typical home, and the City bill for water, wastewater, stormwater and waste, at the same water use.

First, the budget. The City proposes a fifteen percent increase in property tax revenue for twenty twenty-seven. For a typical home, the City says property tax rises from two hundred and twenty-nine dollars a month to two hundred and sixty-six, and water and waste from one hundred and forty to one hundred and fifty-six. That is fifty-three dollars more a month, or about six hundred and thirty dollars a year.
Water is a big part of it. The typical water bill rises about twelve percent next year, mostly for wastewater, as the City upgrades two treatment plants and builds new feedermains.

If the reported tax increases for the following years pass, water rises as Council approved, and cart fees rise as the City proposed, a typical home would pay about five hundred and sixty-seven dollars a month by twenty thirty. That is fifty-four percent more than today, before inflation.

Now, the comparison. In twenty twenty-six, Calgary's three hundred and sixty-nine dollars is the lowest of the eight cities. Saskatoon and Winnipeg are close behind. Vancouver, Edmonton and Ottawa pay the most, more than five hundred dollars a month. The other seven cities average four hundred and sixty-seven.
Calgary is the third lowest on property tax alone, and the third lowest on utilities alone. Together, it comes out lowest.
Against what households earn, Calgarians pay the smallest share of the eight: about four and a half percent of the median household's income.

In twenty twenty-seven, using what other cities have published so far, Calgary would be the third lowest. Its gap below the average would narrow from about ninety-eight dollars a month to about fifty-seven. Toronto, Ottawa and Vancouver have not published their twenty twenty-seven figures yet, and Edmonton's and Regina's are still proposals, so this will change.
One caution. Tax rates on their own mislead. Vancouver has the lowest rate, but its homes are worth far more, so its bills are the highest. What matters is the dollars a household pays.

Every figure comes from each city's own budgets and rate schedules, and every source is published with the study. Read it at calgary insight dot c a. To work out your own bill, enter your home's assessed value at calgary insight dot c a slash bill.
